Apple_Apple Scab.description: A widespread fungal disease affecting apple trees, significantly reducing fruit quality and yield.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves.
Scabby, dark, cracked spots on fruit surfaces.
Premature yellowing and dropping of leaves.
causes: Fungus: Venturia inaequalis.
Overwintered fungal spores on fallen leaf litter.
Prolonged leaf wetness and moderate cool spring temperatures.
treatment: Apply approved organic or chemical copper/sulfur fungicides.
Prune infected branches to eliminate localized spore sources.
prevention: Rake, remove, or bury fallen leaves in autumn.
Plant scab-resistant apple varieties.
Prune canopy thoroughly to improve airflow and rapid drying.

Apple_Black Rot.description: A destructive fungal complex causing leaf spots, cankers on branches, and rotting of fruit.
symptoms: Concentric rings of dark brown decay on the fruit (frog-eye effect).
Small purple spots on upper leaf surfaces that expand with tan centers.
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on bark limbs.
causes: Fungus: Botryosphaeria obtusa.
Spores spreading via water splashes from existing wood cankers.
Warm, humid conditions following rainy periods.
treatment: Prune out dead wood, mummified fruits, and active cankers completely.
Apply target fungicides during the early bud break phase.
prevention: Remove all mummified fruit remaining on trees over winter.
Avoid mechanical damage to bark where spores easily enter.
Burn or deeply bury pruned infected wood away from the orchard.

Apple_Cedar Apple Rust.description: A dual-host fungal disease requiring both apple trees and Eastern Red Cedar to complete its lifecycle.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Small tube-like structures developing under leaves later in summer.
Distorted or dropped fruit with orange lesions.
causes: Fungus: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae.
Spores blowing from nearby cedar galls during warm wet spring weather.
treatment: Apply preventative rust-specific systemic fungicides early in the season.
prevention: Remove nearby wild Eastern Red Cedar trees within a 1-2 mile radius if feasible.
Cultivate rust-resistant apple cultivars.
Apply protective treatments before rainy spring weather arrives.

Apple_Healthy.description: Healthy apple plant showing robust vegetative growth and clear, productive fruit development.
symptoms: Vibrant green uniform leaves with clean margins.
No unusual spotting, discoloration, or structural lesions.
Clean bark and firm, unblemished fruit development.
causes: Optimal soil nutrients and watering practices.
Good preventative pest and disease management programs.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Maintain ongoing structural pruning and balanced irrigation routines.
Monitor periodically for early signs of seasonal pests.

Bell Pepper_Bacterial Spot.description: A severe seed-borne bacterial infection causing complete leaf drops and unmarketable blemished peppers.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked dark spots on lower leaf surfaces.
Spots turn brown, raise slightly, and cause universal yellowing and defoliation.
Rough, raised circular warts appearing on developing peppers.
causes: Bacterium: Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria.
Contaminated seeds, infected crop residues, and overhead irrigation splashes.
High humidity accompanied by warm day temperatures.
treatment: Apply copper-based bacterial sprays early upon identification.
Immediately remove and destroy heavily infested individual plants.
prevention: Utilize certified pathogen-free seeds and disease-resistant transplants.
Practice strict 2-3 year crop rotation skipping solanaceous families.
Switch to drip irrigation systems to keep foliage completely dry.

Bell Pepper_Healthy.description: Healthy pepper plant displaying strong upright stems, vibrant leaves, and high-quality fruit setting.
symptoms: Deep green leaves free from spots or curling.
Sturdy vertical framework with firm, uniform green or red peppers.
causes: Balanced nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium soil ratios.
Adequate sunlight and consistent root moisture zones.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Mulch around bases to stabilize soil conditions.
Maintain standard preventative scouting schedules.

Cherry_Healthy.description: Healthy cherry tree showing robust foliage and smooth trunk development.
symptoms: Lush, uniformly green serrated leaves.
Absence of fungal powdery residues or dark spots.
causes: Favorable winter chilling hours met and adequate spring drainage.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Prune during dry dormant seasons to promote air entry.
Apply standard organic compost mulches annually.

Cherry_Powdery Mildew.description: A fungal disease coating leaves and shoots in a powdery film, leading to distorted leaf growth and reduced photosynthesis.
symptoms: White to light-gray powdery fungal patches on leaves and young shoots.
Upward curling, puckering, and distortion of young leaves.
Stunted seedling growth and unmarketable powdery fruit coatings.
causes: Fungus: Podosphaera clandestina.
High humidity in shaded canopies combined with warm, dry days.
Overwintering fungal mycelium inside dormant tree buds.
treatment: Apply horticultural oils, potassium bicarbonate, or sulfur fungicides.
Prune dense interior shoots to let direct sunlight inside.
prevention: Avoid excessive overhead nitrogen fertilization that forces soft, susceptible growth.
Space trees adequately to maximize environmental ventilation.

Corn (Maize)_Cercospora Leaf Spot.description: Commonly known as Gray Leaf Spot, this fungal disease creates extensive leaf lesions that severely impact grain filling.
symptoms: Long, narrow, rectangular tan-to-gray spots running parallel to leaf veins.
Lesions merge, turning entire leaves brown and dry.
Severe premature plant death and stalk lodging.
causes: Fungus: Cercospora zeae-maydis.
High relative humidity and extended periods of dew on leaves.
Spore survival on minimal-till corn debris remaining on soil surfaces.
treatment: Apply foliar strobilurin or triazole fungicides at the silking stage if thresholds are breached.
prevention: Rotate field out of corn to non-host crops like soybeans for 1-2 years.
Plant hybrid corn varieties with documented gray leaf spot resistance.
Deep plow infected debris to accelerate organic breakdown.

Corn (Maize)_Common Rust.description: A fungal rust disease characterized by distinct powdery pustules that strip nutrients from maize plants.
symptoms: Elongated golden-brown to cinnamon-colored powdery pustules on both leaf sides.
Pustules turn dark brown to black late in the season.
Leaf yellowing and premature drying under high infestation.
causes: Fungus: Puccinia sorghi.
Windblown spores arriving from southern overwintering regions.
Cool temperatures combined with high humidity or frequent dews.
treatment: Fungicide sprays are rarely needed unless severe infection strikes susceptible inbred lines early.
prevention: Select and plant common-rust resistant maize hybrids.
Adjust planting dates to avoid high-risk early season moisture windows.

Corn (Maize)_Healthy.description: Healthy maize plant presenting sturdy stalks and optimal photosynthetic surface area.
symptoms: Broad, dark green uniform leaves free from linear lesions.
Thick, resilient structural stalks and uniform ear development.
causes: Proper seed-bed prep, ideal crop rotation, and optimal macro-nutrient levels.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Maintain soil health through integrated cover cropping and balanced fertilization.

Corn (Maize)_Northern Leaf Blight.description: A serious fungal disease producing large cigar-shaped lesions that can cause extensive defoliation.
symptoms: Large, elongated, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions (1-6 inches long).
Lesions start on lower leaves and progress rapidly upward.
Dirty, dark dusty appearance within lesions during wet weather due to spore production.
causes: Fungus: Exserohilum turcicum.
Overwintered spores on unburied field debris.
Moderate temperatures paired with prolonged wet conditions.
treatment: Apply economic foliar fungicides prior to or during the tasseling stage if necessary.
prevention: Utilize hybrids with strong Ht-gene specific resistance.
Implement thorough field tillage to bury infested residue.
Practice crop rotation to interrupt the fungal life cycle.

Grape_Black Rot.description: A highly destructive grape fungal disease capable of rotting entire berry clusters under favorable weather.
symptoms: Small, circular cream-colored spots with dark brown borders on leaves.
Berries turn pale dot-like tan, rapidly shriveling into hard, black, wrinkled mummies.
Black pimple-like fruiting bodies forming on mummified fruit.
causes: Fungus: Guignardia bidwellii.
Spores overwintering inside abandoned, dried fruit mummies on vines or soil.
Warm, wet spring and summer weather conditions.
treatment: Apply targeted protectant fungicides starting from early bloom through fruit set.
Remove and discard infected fruit clusters instantly.
prevention: Prune and destroy all mummified berries from the trellis every winter.
Keep canopy widely spaced and weeded around the base for airflow.
Select resistant cultivars if establishing new vineyard blocks.

Grape_Esca (Black Measles).description: A complex, slow-moving wood disease caused by wood-boring fungi, affecting grape yields and vine longevity.
symptoms: Interveinal leaf tissue yellowing and drying out, forming a 'tiger-stripe' pattern.
Dark purple spots or flecks distributed across the skin of developing grapes.
Stunted growth, vine wilting, and internal dark wood streaking.
causes: Fungi complex including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium aleophilum.
Infection entering through open structural pruning wounds during wet seasons.
treatment: There are no highly effective chemical cures; prune infected arms down to clean wood.
Apply protective wound sealants to major pruning cuts.
prevention: Prune strictly during dry, late-winter weather windows.
Disinfect pruning shears regularly between individual vines.
Replace declining, heavily infected vines to preserve vineyard health.

Grape_Healthy.description: Healthy grape vine showing uniform leaf growth and clear, unblemished fruit clusters.
symptoms: Unblemished green leaves with standard scalloped shapes.
Uniform fruit setting with smooth skins and clear internal wood.
causes: Well-drained soil, correct trellising, and proactive preventative management.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Adhere to routine nitrogen management and structural winter training protocols.

Grape_Leaf Blight.description: A late-season fungal disease targeting mature leaves, leading to isolated early leaf drops.
symptoms: Dull, dark brown irregular spots on older foliage.
Leaf margins drying up, curling, and breaking off.
Premature defoliation resulting in sun-scalded grape clusters.
causes: Fungus: Pseudocercospora vitis.
Humid late-summer conditions paired with weak or nutrient-stressed vines.
treatment: Apply standard copper or broad-spectrum fungicides if disease presents early in summer.
prevention: Maintain overall vine vigor through strategic irrigation and fertilization.
Clean up fallen leaf debris post-harvest to reduce spring inoculum levels.

Peach_Bacterial Spot.description: A bacterial disease causing stone fruit damage, leaf spotting, and early defoliation.
symptoms: Small, pale-green spots on leaves that turn purple-brown and fall out, creating a 'shot-hole' look.
Severe yellowing of leaf tips followed by quick dropping.
Deep, dark, pitted cracks and lesions on peach skin.
causes: Bacterium: Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni.
Bacterial overwintering in twig cankers and bud scales.
Spring rains, driving winds, and warm humid orchard temperatures.
treatment: Apply preventative copper sprays or oxytetracycline during the dormant and shuck-split phases.
prevention: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which creates highly vulnerable succulent shoots.
Plant less-susceptible peach cultivars.
Incorporate windbreaks to limit wind-driven bacterial spread across blocks.

Peach_Healthy.description: Healthy peach tree displaying active structural development and clear stone fruit skin.
symptoms: Clean lanceolate green leaves devoid of perforations or spots.
Smooth bark and fuzzy, unblemished developing peach fruit.
causes: Adequate winter chilling hours, deep sandy loam soils, and proper pruning.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Maintain orchard sanitation and balanced spring nitrogen regimes.

Potato_Early Blight.description: A fungal disease creating target-board spots on older potato leaves, reducing tuber sizes.
symptoms: Dark brown, circular spots with concentric rings ('target' look) on older leaves.
Yellow borders surrounding leaf spots as they expand.
Sunken, leathery, brown lesions on harvested potato tubers.
causes: Fungus: Alternaria solani.
Fungal survival on old solanaceous crop residues or alternative weed hosts.
Alternating periods of morning dew/wetness and hot, dry afternoon weather.
treatment: Apply protective or systemic fungicides when lower leaf spotting begins.
prevention: Implement a strict 3-year field rotation excluding potatoes, tomatoes, and peppers.
Maintain optimal soil fertility, particularly nitrogen and potassium, to prevent plant stress.
Avoid overhead irrigation methods to decrease leaf wetness duration.

Potato_Healthy.description: Healthy potato crop showing vigorous bushy green canopy and strong underground tuber development.
symptoms: Lush, upright green foliage without target spots or water-soaked rotting.
Firm, solid stems and clear skin on growing underground tubers.
causes: Pathogen-free certified seed tubers, well-drained hilled soils, and dry foliage.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Follow routine hilling schedules and implement clean equipment sanitization protocols.

Potato_Late Blight.description: A highly destructive disease capable of rapidly wiping out entire fields and rotting tubers in storage.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked dark green to black lesions starting at leaf tips.
White, fuzzy fungal-like growth under leaves in humid weather.
Rapid plant collapse accompanied by a distinct foul, decaying odor.
causes: Oomycete: Phytophthora infestans.
Infected seed tubers, cull piles, or windblown spores from nearby fields.
Cool, consistently wet, and highly humid weather conditions.
treatment: Apply specific anti-oomycete systemic fungicides immediately upon local alert warnings.
Destroy all infected plants in the immediate vicinity to halt explosive secondary spreading.
prevention: Plant exclusively certified pathogen-free seed potatoes.
Eliminate all voluntary potato plants and field cull piles before spring planting.
Kill vines completely 2 weeks prior to harvesting to prevent tuber contamination.

Strawberry_Healthy.description: Healthy strawberry plant showing strong crown growth, clear runner development, and high-quality fruit.
symptoms: Vibrant, dark green trifoliate leaves with clean edges.
Bright white blossoms and clean, glossy red berries free from mold.
causes: Adequate mulch protection, well-drained sandy beds, and targeted root irrigation.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Apply straw mulch around bases to isolate ripening fruit from bare soil contact.

Strawberry_Leaf Scorch.description: A common fungal disease of strawberry leaves that reduces plant vigor and winter hardiness.
symptoms: Numerous small, irregular purplish spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Spots expand and merge, causing entire leaves to look scorched, dry, and brown.
Girdled fruit stems leading to small, dried, unmarketable strawberries.
causes: Fungus: Diplocarpon earlianum.
Spores overwintering on old living leaves or fallen crop residue.
Extended rainy periods or frequent overhead irrigation in late spring.
treatment: Apply defensive fungicides early in spring before blooms open if history suggests high pressure.
prevention: Keep plantings thinned out and weeded to maximize airflow.
Mow down beds and destroy old leaves immediately after harvest seasons close.
Choose resistant varieties for wet field areas.

Tomato_Bacterial Spot.description: A seed-borne bacterial disease that creates dark blemishes on fruit and causes severe early leaf drop.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy circular spots on leaves surrounded by yellow halos.
Centers of leaf spots dry out and tear, creating a ragged appearance.
Small, raised, scab-like black spots with light borders on tomato fruits.
causes: Bacterium: Xanthomonas perforans.
Infested commercial seeds, infected volunteer plants, or wind-driven rain splashes.
High temperatures accompanied by high relative humidity levels.
treatment: Apply protective copper-mancozeb tank mixes at weekly intervals.
Prune off lower infected leaf structures during dry afternoons.
prevention: Purchase strictly certified pathogen-free seeds or hot-water treated seeds.
Enforce a 2-year crop rotation away from solanaceous plants.
Sanitize all stakes, cages, and tools thoroughly with disinfectant between seasons.

Tomato_Early Blight.description: A common fungal disease causing target-like spots starting on lower leaves and moving up the plant.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with prominent concentric rings (target pattern) on older leaves.
Lower leaves turn completely yellow and drop off, leaving fruit exposed to sun-scald.
Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at the stem-end of tomato fruit.
causes: Fungus: Alternaria solani.
Overwintered spores on old tomato vines or soil surfaces.
Warm temperatures paired with frequent rainy or humid weather conditions.
treatment: Apply chlorothalonil, copper, or systemic fungicides upon observing early lower spots.
prevention: Prune off lower branches up to 12 inches off the ground to prevent soil spore splash.
Apply thick organic or plastic mulch around the plant base.
Water strictly at ground level using drip lines or soaker hoses.

Tomato_Healthy.description: Healthy tomato plant showing vigorous branching, clean leaves, and consistent fruit clusters.
symptoms: Lush green foliage without interveinal yellowing, spots, or leaf curling.
Sturdy main stems supporting plump, uniformly colored, unblemished fruit.
causes: Adequate calcium levels preventing blossom end rot, and uniform watering.
treatment: No therapeutic treatments required.
prevention: Maintain consistent staking techniques and monitor weekly for early pest presence.

Tomato_Late Blight.description: A destructive oomycete disease capable of rapidly destroying tomato crops within days during wet conditions.
symptoms: Large, rapidly expanding dark greasy-looking spots on leaves and stems.
White, velvety fungal-like growth appearing underneath leaves in damp environments.
Large, firm, greasy golden-brown glossy spots covering whole fruits.
causes: Oomycete: Phytophthora infestans.
Spore travel via wind currents over long distances during cool, cloudy, wet weather.
treatment: Apply dedicated preventative or curative anti-late blight fungicides immediately.
Uproot and bag entire infected plants to prevent airborne spore plumes.
prevention: Avoid planting tomatoes near potato fields.
Monitor regional agricultural extension late-blight trackers daily.
Select late-blight resistant tomato varieties.

Tomato_Septoria Leaf Spot.description: A highly destructive fungal disease that targets tomato leaves, causing severe defoliation from the base upward.
symptoms: Numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and gray centers.
Tiny black specks (fruiting bodies) visible within the gray centers.
Leaves yellow rapidly, wither, and drop off in massive quantities.
causes: Fungus: Septoria lycopersici.
Spores splashing from infected soil onto lower leaves.
Warm, wet, and humid environments over consecutive days.
treatment: Apply copper or chlorothalonil-based protective fungicides on a strict schedule.
prevention: Mulch heavily around the plant base to create a physical barrier against soil splashes.
Prune lower leaves early to eliminate contact with soil surfaces.
Destroy all old tomato frames and debris at the end of the harvest cycle.

Tomato_Yellow Leaf Curl Virus.description: A severe viral disease transmitted by whiteflies that severely stunts plant growth and halts fruit production.
symptoms: Severe stunting of the plant, presenting a bushy, compacted growth pattern.
Leaves curl strongly upward and inward, developing prominent yellow margins.
Flowers drop off prematurely, resulting in little to no fruit set.
causes: Virus: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV).
Transmission via silverleaf whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
Alternative weed hosts keeping viral reservoirs active between planting cycles.
treatment: There are no chemical or viral cures; instantly remove and destroy infected plants.
Apply insecticidal soaps or neem oil to suppress active whitefly populations.
prevention: Grow crops under protective fine-mesh insect netting during early seedling stages.
Use reflective silver mulches to repel invading whiteflies.
Plant certified TYLCV-resistant tomato cultivars.
